content: The Vessel Sanitation Program (VSP) acknowledges the contributions of various organizations and companies in revising the VSP 2011 Construction Guidelines. The cover art for the guidelines was designed by Carrie Green. The Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) established the Vessel Sanitation Program (VSP) in 1975 as a collaborative initiative with the cruise vessel industry. The primary objective of the VSP is to assist the cruise industry in developing and implementing comprehensive sanitation programs to safeguard the health of passengers and crew aboard cruise vessels. Cruise vessels are subject to biannual operational inspections and, if necessary, reinspections conducted by the VSP. Vessel owners are required to pay a fee for these inspections, which is determined based on the vessel's gross registered tonnage (GRT). Details of these inspections are outlined in the VSP guidelines. Cruise vessel owners or shipyards involved in building or renovating cruise vessels may voluntarily request plan reviews, on-site shipyard construction inspections, and/or final construction inspections before the vessel's first or next operational inspection. Fees for on-site and final construction inspections are also based on the vessel's GRT, but no fees are charged for plan reviews or consultations. If a plan review or construction inspection is requested, the VSP reviews the shipyard or owner's current construction billing invoices. If invoices remain unpaid for more than 90 days, no inspection will be scheduled until the outstanding invoices are fully paid. The VSP 2011 Construction Guidelines provide a consistent framework for construction and design standards that protect the health of passengers and crew. The CDC is committed to promoting high construction standards to ensure public health. Compliance with these guidelines helps maintain a healthy environment on cruise vessels. The guidelines cover various aspects of a vessel's facilities related to public health, including food storage, preparation, and service, as well as water bunkering, storage, disinfection, and distribution. Vessel owners and operators are free to select designs and equipment that meet their needs, provided they also comply with the sanitary design criteria of the American National Standards Institute (ANSI) or equivalent organizations, as well as VSP's operational inspection requirements. The guidelines are not intended to restrict the introduction of new designs, materials, or technologies in shipbuilding. Shipbuilders, owners, manufacturers, or other interested parties may request periodic reviews or revisions of the guidelines to incorporate new information or technology. The guidelines also align with international maritime conventions, such as the Safety of Life at Sea Convention, the International Convention for the Prevention of Pollution from Ships, and others. The VSP 2011 Construction Guidelines became effective on September 15, 2011. They apply to all structural changes made to vessels after this date but do not apply to minor renovations, such as the installation or removal of single pieces of equipment or single pipe runs. The guidelines are applicable to all areas of the vessel affected by a renovation. During routine vessel sanitation inspections and reinspections, the VSP inspects the entire vessel in accordance with the VSP 2011 Operations Manual. The VSP periodically reviews and revises its recommendations in collaboration with industry representatives and other stakeholders to keep pace with industry innovations. Shipbuilders, owners, manufacturers, or other interested parties may request a review of a construction guideline based on new technologies, concepts, or methods. Recommendations for changes should identify the section to be revised, describe the proposed change, state the reason for the change, and include supporting research or test results. The VSP evaluates these recommendations in consultation with industry professionals to determine whether to include them in the next revision. To request plan reviews, consultations, or construction-related inspections, an official written request must be submitted to the VSP Chief as early as possible in the planning, construction, or renovation process. Requests requiring foreign travel must be submitted at least 45 days before the intended visit. The VSP assigns primary and secondary officers to coordinate with the vessel owner and shipyard. These officers serve as points of contact throughout the process, from plan review to final construction inspection. Vessel representatives should also designate points of contact to represent the owners, shipyard, and key subcontractors. Plan reviews for new construction are typically conducted at least 18 months before the vessel's scheduled delivery. Major renovations require varying timelines, and the VSP coordinates plan reviews well in advance of the work. Plan reviews usually take two working days and are conducted in Atlanta, Georgia; Fort Lauderdale, Florida; or other agreed-upon locations. Representatives from the shipyard, vessel owner, and subcontractors should attend the review and bring all relevant materials, including complete plans, equipment specifications, and other pertinent documents. The VSP prepares a plan review report summarizing recommendations made during the review and submits it to the shipyard and owner representatives. Following the review, the shipyard must provide any redrawn plans and copies of major change orders. During construction, shipyard representatives or vessel representatives may direct questions or requests for consultative services to the VSP project officers in writing. On-site construction inspections are typically conducted in shipyards outside the United States. Shipyards are encouraged to coordinate with the VSP Chief well in advance of the 45-day minimum to better plan inspection dates. On-site inspections generally require one to three officers, depending on the vessel's size and design. These inspections, including travel, usually take five working days and should be conducted approximately four to five weeks before the vessel's delivery when 90% of the areas to be inspected are completed. A written report is provided to the requesting party, and the shipyard must submit a corrective action statement addressing each item identified in the inspection report before the ship's arrival in the United States. Final construction inspections are conducted at the request of a vessel owner or shipyard only after construction is 100% complete and the ship is fully operational. These inspections evaluate findings from previous yard inspections, assess incomplete areas, and test systems that could not be tested earlier. Systems tested include ventilation, warewash machines, artificial light levels, temperature controls, and water chemistry measures. A formal written request for a final construction inspection must be submitted to the VSP Chief as soon as possible after the vessel is completed or at least 10 days before its arrival in the United States. After the inspection, the shipyard must submit a corrective action statement outlining how it will address each cited item and the projected completion date. Vessels undergoing final construction inspections in the United States are generally scheduled for an unannounced operational inspection within four weeks of the final construction inspection. If no final construction inspection is requested, an unannounced operational inspection is conducted within four weeks of the vessel's arrival in the United States. These inspections are conducted in accordance with the VSP 2011 Operations Manual. The VSP does not test, certify, or endorse equipment or materials used by the cruise industry. Instead, it recognizes certifications from independent testing laboratories such as NSF International, Underwriter's Laboratories (UL), and ANSI. Equipment built to questionable standards is reviewed by a committee consisting of VSP, cruise ship industry, and independent testing organization participants to determine compliance with recommended standards. Equipment manufacturers and suppliers should not contact the VSP for product approval. The VSP 2011 Construction Guidelines include definitions to clarify commonly used terminology. Definitions are organized alphabetically, and terms identified in the text are presented in small capital letters. Examples of defined terms include accessible, air gap, backflow prevention, black water, blast chiller, and food-contact surface. These definitions ensure consistent understanding and application of the guidelines.
